title: Noach: ten generations of waiting (Avot 5:2)
hookLine: from Noah to Abraham ten generations pass with no one turning
tomorrow: Lech Lecha: the road ran everywhere

lines: LISTS OF NAMES, EASY TO SKIM.
cards: Some changes move slower than a lifetime. A habit that won't break. A family pattern that shows up in the grandparents, then the parents, then the kids.
A cause that moves an inch a decade. After long enough, it starts to sound like this: if it hasn't changed by now, it never will.
The end of the portion of Noah is mostly lists of names: nations, cities, a tower that never gets finished, then more names. It's easy to skim.
But a teaching in Pirkei Avot counts those names, and finds something in them about waiting.

teach.h: TEN GENERATIONS FROM ADAM TO NOAH.
teach.b: Pirkei Avot says: there were ten generations from Adam to Noah, to show how patient God is. All those generations kept provoking God, until God brought the flood.
Then ten generations from Noah to Abraham, to show how patient God is.
All those generations kept provoking God, until Abraham came and received the reward of them all. Ten generations, twice over. A long wait for one person to turn.
And the two lists end differently: the first in a flood, the second in Abraham. Same patience, different ending. What changed?
Someone finally turned. The portion itself shows the waiting.
After the flood, people build a city and a tower to reach the heavens, to make a name for themselves, and God scatters them. Then come the names again. And at the very end, a small detail.

teach.h: TERAH SETS OUT, AND STOPS IN HARAN.
teach.b: Abraham's father, Terah, takes his family and sets out from Ur toward the land of Canaan. They get as far as Haran, and stop, and settle there. Terah dies in Haran.
He was headed in the right direction, and didn't arrive.
The next portion begins with his son picking up the road. So this portion ends in the middle of a journey. That's what a slow change looks like here: generation after generation, and nothing.
A father who starts and stops. Then a son who keeps going.

how: Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, is often studied on Shabbat afternoons; its fifth chapter's teachings on the ten generations are read alongside the genealogies at the end of the portion of Noach.

o: Noah, the portion from the flood to Terah
the tower built to make a name for themselves
the ark's window, opened to send the dove

games.q: the long wait — tap the pairs.
p: a name for themselves, then scattered
set out for Canaan, stopped in Haran

s: Pirkei Avot says the ten generations show God's patience
both lists of ten, it says, show how patient God is.
Terah reached the land of Canaan
he set out toward it, stopped in Haran, and died there.
both sets of ten generations end in a flood
the first ends in the flood; the second ends when Abraham comes.

games.q: you're Terah. you've set out from Ur with your family, headed for Canaan. you reach Haran. what does the Torah say you do?
games.why: Terah settles in Haran and dies there. the next portion begins with his son picking up the road.

practice: Think of one change you've been waiting for, in yourself or in someone you love, and notice the impatience: the sigh, the it'll never happen. Let it be there, then remember Terah stopping in Haran, and his son picking up the road.
Maybe you're the one who starts, maybe the one who keeps going; either way, the road isn't wasted.

wordCard.voice: Noach. The portion of Noah: a whole-hearted man, a window, laws for everyone, a cloak, and ten generations of waiting.

orig.note: Hebrew: generations; the singular is dor.

carryVoice: Your line: ten generations. And with that, the portion of Noah is done. Tomorrow, the road picks up again.
